analysis.one_liner: Removes the exemption letting natural gas drillers frack without federal drinking-water oversight and forces public disclosure of the chemicals they use.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and its Energy and Environment Subcommittee, never received a hearing or a vote, and died when the 111th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Fracking injects water, sand, and chemicals underground to release natural gas. A 2005 law exempted fracking from the Safe Drinking Water Act, so drillers did not need federal permits for fluids injected near drinking water sources and did not have to say what chemicals they used. This bill would have repealed that exemption and required companies to disclose their fracking chemicals to states, which would have to post the information online, while still protecting trade-secret formulas and allowing doctors access in medical emergencies.
analysis.who_benefits: People who live near oil and gas drilling, especially those relying on private wells or groundwater. They would gain federal oversight of fluids injected underground near drinking water and a public list of the chemicals used in nearby fracking operations, with doctors able to get chemical identities in an emergency.

how_it_helps.text: It closes the legal loophole that currently leaves hydraulic fracturing—the injection of chemical-laden fluids into the ground near oil and gas wells—outside the Safe Drinking Water Act's permitting rules.
It requires drilling companies to tell state regulators which chemicals they use in fracking, and requires states to post that information publicly on the internet.
It lets a treating physician or nurse get the specific chemical identity—even a trade-secret formula—in a medical emergency, without waiting for a confidentiality agreement.

analysis.who_pays: Oil and gas companies, which would face federal permitting under the Safe Drinking Water Act and mandatory public disclosure of fracturing chemicals, plus compliance costs that could be passed to consumers through energy prices.

drawbacks.text: Subjecting hydraulic fracturing to Safe Drinking Water Act underground-injection permitting could add regulatory costs and delays for oil and gas production, which industry argued could raise energy costs and slow domestic gas development.

Even with the trade-secret protections in the bill—disclosure of chemical constituents but not proprietary formulas, and emergency disclosure to treating physicians—public posting of chemical identities on the internet raised competitive-confidentiality concerns for drilling companies.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits—protecting drinking-water sources and giving the public information about chemicals pumped underground—were broad, while the costs fell on a narrow set of oil and gas producers. The main good-faith objection is that federal permitting could add delay and expense to drilling and that full public disclosure could expose trade-secret formulas; the bill tried to address this by requiring disclosure of chemical constituents but not proprietary formulas, with emergency medical disclosure carve-outs. The bill still died without a hearing or a vote, so its real-world costs and benefits were never tested in the legislative process.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and then to a subcommittee, where it sat without a hearing or vote until Congress adjourned.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on June 9, 2009 by Rep. Diana DeGette with 72 cosponsors, including one Republican.
It was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce on June 9, 2009, and the next day to the Subcommittee on Energy and Environment.
No further action was taken; the bill never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil and gas drilling companies, which kept their exemption from federal drinking-water regulation and faced no chemical disclosure requirement; no states or residents gained any new protections.

for.name: Rep. Diana DeGette (D-CO)
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to repeal the fracking exemption and require chemical disclosure.

against.name: House Committee on Energy and Commerce
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and took no action—hearing, markup, or vote—before the Congress ended.

against.name: Oil and gas industry
against.role: Hydraulic fracturing companies and trade groups
against.what_they_did: Opposed federal regulation of fracking and disclosure of fracturing chemicals.

sides.party_line_note: All 72 cosponsors were Democrats except one Republican; with Democrats controlling both chambers, the bill's failure to move reflected committee inaction rather than a floor vote.

industries.note: The bill would have ended their exemption from Safe Drinking Water Act underground-injection rules and required them to disclose fracking chemicals publicly, adding permitting and compliance costs.

industries.industry: Chemical suppliers to the fracking industry
industries.note: Their chemicals would have had to be identified publicly, limiting secrecy around fracturing fluid contents.
